paras: The lynching of a sheepman in Harney Valley, Oregon, was a killing reported in early January 1888, in which an unnamed sheepman said to have killed a cattleman was himself lynched. A dispatch from The Dalles described the two deaths as a "double homicide" growing out of a quarrel between cattle and sheep men. The only known report is a two-sentence item in the Los Angeles Daily Herald, which gives no names, date or account of the lynchers.
According to the dispatch, the violence came out of "a quarrel between cattle and sheep men" in Harney Valley. The item does not say what the quarrel was about or how long it had gone on.

One of the sheep men killed one of the cattle men, and the sheepman "was in turn lynched," in the words of the report. The dispatch added that "his sheep are scattered all over the country." It does not name either man, give the race of either, say who carried out the lynching, or describe how it was done.
No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution appears in the coverage found.

The Los Angeles Daily Herald printed the story on January 10, 1888, on its front page in a column of Pacific Northwest news headed "Notes From the North," under a Portland dateline of January 9. The Harney Valley item followed a report of a fatal house fire in Powder River Valley and ran without a headline or comment of its own. It presented the lynching as the closing turn of a range quarrel rather than as a matter of race or law enforcement.
No Oregon paper's version of the story and no Black-press account appear in the coverage.
